id=\"post-body-4117639046604444703\"\u003EOsce questions : \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp;\u003Cb\u003E \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; 1) Dialysis Disequilibrium syndrome? \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u003C\/b\u003E\u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp;\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"post-body entry-content float-container\" id=\"post-body-4117639046604444703\"\u003E\u0026nbsp;\u0026nbsp;\u0026nbsp;Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome (DDS) refers to an array of neurological manifestations seen during or following dialysis, primarily after the new initiation of dialysis.However, it can also be seen in chronic dialysis patients who miss their regular dialysis treatments. This syndrome is thought to arise from fluid shifts during hemodialysis, causing cerebral edema and a wide variety of neurological symptoms. In continuous renal replacement therapies (CRRT), where fluid shift is limited, dialysis disequilibrium syndrome is rarely reported.\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EThe common risk factors that predispose a patient to dialysis dysequilibrium syndrome are\u0026nbsp;\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EFirst hemodialysis treatment\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EHigh blood urea nitrogen (BUN) (above 175 mg\/dL or 60 mmol\/L) before initiation of dialysis\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EExtremes of age – children and elderly\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003ESudden change in dialysis regimen\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EPre-existing neurological diseases such as stroke, malignant hypertension, head trauma, or seizure disorder\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EPresence of other conditions causing cerebral edema (hyponatremia, hepatic encephalopathy)\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EConditions causing increased permeability of the blood-brain barrier (sepsis, meningitis, encephalitis, hemolytic uremic syndrome, vasculitis) \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp;\u003Cb\u003E2) How spironolactone cause gynecomastea\u003C\/b\u003E? \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp; Spironolactone induces gynecomastia by decreasing testosterone production, increasing peripheral conversion of testosterone to estradiol, and displacing estradiol from sex hormone-binding globulin.\u0026nbsp;\u003C\/div\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"post-bottom\"\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"post-footer float-container\"\u003E\u003Cdiv class=\"post-footer-line An informed consent was taken from patient\/ attender and there is omission of information that was requested to be omitted\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EA 60 year old male, who is a resident of Nalgonda ,farmer by occupation came with\u0026nbsp;\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u0026nbsp;\u003Cb\u003EChief complaints:\u003C\/b\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E-Pedal edema since 3 months\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E-shortness of breath since 20 days\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E- decreased\u0026nbsp; urine output since 15 days\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cb\u003EHistory of presenting illness:\u003C\/b\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EThe patient was apparently asymptomatic 3 months back when he noticed\u0026nbsp; bilateral pedal edema initially extending to ankle Gradually progressed up to thighs which worsened during last 15 days.\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E-Decreased urine output since 15 days, not associated with frequency, urgency burning micturation.\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E-Grade 3 shortness of breath, no aggravating and relieving factors.\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cb\u003E\u003Ci\u003ESeries of events :\u003C\/i\u003E\u003C\/b\u003E-\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EHistory of trauma by fall from tree 17\u0026nbsp; years back, where he used NSAIDS for 4\/5 yrs .. and then 12 years back he developed pedal edema where he got diagnosed that he had kidney problems and he was on medication for where edema was subsided and it was more recurrent on those 5 years.\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EAnd after that 2 years later he got scrotal swelling ( which may be due to generalised anasarca)which got infected followed by trauma which was associated with fever and pain then he was diagnosed with ckd\u0026nbsp; \u0026nbsp;For which he got treated by dailysis initially and then he started using medications and was apparently well till 3 months back\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E3 months back patient developed bilateral pedal edema, facial puffiness for the first time and shortness of breath so he visited local hospital and they referred to our hospital for dailysis.\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003ESince then patient was coming here regularly twice a weak for dialysis .\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003EAfter his last dialysis session he went back home and he developed discomfort in chest and weakness of limbs . Patient also had few episodes of altered sensorium in between which was associated with fever and chills .So he was brought to hospital again.\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cbr\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\u003Cdiv\u003E\u003Cb\u003EPAST
